parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

{align=center} **Vegetable Palace (VP) **

VP was started 10 years ago in country Z. It is a public limited company. VP has a chain of 500 fast-food restaurants that operate across country Z. The VP brand is famous for its vegetarian food, this means none of its meals contain meat. 

VP has a head office in Main City where all the directors and senior managers work. There are many barriers to communication. Each VP restaurant has a Manager, an Assistant Manager and 50 employees who cook and serve the meals. Restaurant Managers are often very busy and they are considering delegating some of their tasks to the Assistant Managers. 

The ingredients for the restaurants are ordered in bulk by head office and then distributed from its warehouse to each of the restaurants. However, some senior managers think that Restaurant Managers should purchase their own ingredients from local suppliers. This would mean the ingredients would be fresher and would allow variations in the meals served.

VP wants to expand into another country. It will choose between the two countries shown in Appendix 2. VP will also need to decide how to enter a new market in another country. It has the option of forming a joint venture with another business or franchising the VP brand. The choice of finance will need to be considered for the expansion and the amount of finance will depend on the option chosen.

{align=center} **Appendix 1 **

{align=center} **Advertisement for VP's restaurants**

{align=center} Choose VP for the finest vegetarian meals. Our service is the fastest possible! 

{align=center} You will receive your meal in less than 5 minutes – guaranteed! 

{align=center} Delicious and varied meals for even the biggest of appetites and all at competitive prices. 

{align=center} New meals are being introduced all the time. 

{align=center} There is a VP restaurant near you – we look forward to serving you soon

{align=center} **Appendix 2 **

{align=center} **Summary of the two possible countries that VP could choose to locate its new restaurants.**

|   | ** Country A** | ** Country B** |
| --- | :---: | :---: |
| **Raw materials** | Average variable cost \$6 per meal | Average variable cost \$2 per meal |
| **Labour** | Low unemployment \$10 per hour for each employee | High unemployment \$5 per hour for each employee |
| **Market** | Many competitors Average price per meal = \$20 | Few competitors Average price per meal = \$10 |

{align=center} **Appendix 3 **

{align=center} **Email from VP’s Managing Director to VP’s Marketing Director**

To: VP’s Marketing Director 

From: VP’s Managing Director 

Date: 31 March 2023 

Re: Economic changes in country Z 

Did you see the news this morning that interest rates will be raised from 3% to 5% later today? This will have several effects on our business in country Z. 

The news also said that the exchange rate in country Z has depreciated. We will have to consider how this will affect our business, especially as we import 30% of our ingredients into country Z. 

There are also new legal controls being introduced that mean we have to list all the ingredients used in each of our meals on the menu. We do reprint menus every time we change the meals, but it is something to consider. 

Speak later today.

Consider the following **two **ways VP can purchase its inventory.

- Head Office purchases the inventory for all the restaurants.
- Restaurant managers purchase their own inventory from local suppliers.

Which way should it use? Justify your answer.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/jun-2023-paper-2-case-study---new.pdf)when answering the question.
parts.solution_md:
Centralised purchasing by Head Office allows VP to benefit from bulk discounts, lowering food costs across its restaurants. Lower costs could provide more financial flexibility **[An]** for the planned expansion into another country **[Ap]**. Centralised purchasing also ensures consistency** **in ingredients, maintaining VP's brand reputation **[An] **for quality vegetarian meals served in under 5 minutes **[Ap]**, as advertised

However, allowing restaurant managers to purchase from local suppliers could result in fresher ingredients and allow for meal variation **[Ap]**. This could help VP compete more effectively, especially if they expand into countries with different tastes **[An]**. Restaurant managers are already very busy **[Ap]**, so adding purchasing responsibilities could overburden them and lead to poor decision-making, which could affect restaurant performance **[An]**

VP should continue with centralised purchasing by Head Office **[E]**. The cost savings from bulk ordering are likely to be significant for the chain of 500 restaurants **[Ap]**, especially considering the potential impact of a depreciating exchange rate **[Ap]**. Consistency is also crucial for a fast-food brand **[E]**. Customers expect the same taste and quality at every VP location. Allowing busy restaurant managers **[Ap] **to organise purchasing of ingredients may not guarantee this consistency, which could affect the reputation of the national brand **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Head office buys inventory for every restaurant**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Bulk buying of ingredients → supplier discounts → lower unit cost → higher profit
>     - Same suppliers for all outlets → meals stay consistent → good brand reputation
>     - Head office can set quality standards → easier to control food safety
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Extra transport needed to deliver to each branch → higher distribution cost
>     - Warehouse space required before shipping to outlets → adds rent and handling cost
> - **Restaurant Managers buy from local suppliers**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Managers choose ingredients that match local tastes → attracts more customers
>     - Frequent local deliveries → fresher stock → better food quality
>     - Responsibility motivates managers → feel trusted and engaged
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Busy managers may forget or delay orders → risk of stock-outs and lost sales
>     - Some ingredients unavailable locally → full menu not always offered
>     - No bulk discount → higher ingredient cost → lower profit per meal
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - Head office buying saves money through economies of scale and keeps quality uniform but raises storage and transport costs
>   - Local buying lets each restaurant meet local demand quickly and boosts manager motivation but loses bulk discounts and may cause stock gaps

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

{align=center} **MainCity Bakery (MB)**

MainCity Bakery (MB) MB is a small bakery that produces bread. Yasin started the bakery 6 months ago with help from the government. Yasin needed a business plan to support his application for government help. An extract from the business plan Yasin produced is shown in Appendix 1. The market research was carried out by Yasin. He asked a small sample of family and friends to fill in a questionnaire. Yasin’s business plan also contained forecast data. MB’s bread is freshly-made every day in the bakery, which is located at the back of MB’s small shop. The bread is then sold the same day. Yasin has 2 employees to help him produce the bread and 1 employee to serve customers in the shop. All employees work 5 days a week and are paid the legal minimum wage. Yasin uses a democratic leadership style. Yasin needs to keep costs low to be competitive. He uses packaging that cannot be recycled. Yasin also buys the cheapest ingredients, most of which are imported. He is planning to use lean production in the bakery but he has to decide which method to use. MB’s main competitors advertise that they only use ingredients from local suppliers. Yasin is thinking of changing the suppliers he uses for ingredients and packaging. He wants MB to have a good ethical image which he could use in advertising. Yasin plans to start making cakes. He is considering two options as outlined in Appendix 2. MB’s fixed costs will increase as there will be additional expenses whichever option he chooses.

{align=center} 

{align=center} **Appendix 1 **

{align=center} **Extract from Yasin’s business plan for MB**

| Section | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Market research | Questionnaire results are as follows:- Bread is eaten by all age groups
- Of the sample asked:
- 85% want products made using ingredients from local suppliers
- 70% want to purchase cakes as well as bread from a bakery |
| Resources | - \$10 000 to buy bakery equipment
- Rent for the bakery and shop each month
- \$3000 for start-up supplies and ingredients |

{align=center} 

{align=center} **Appendix 2**

{align=center} **Forecast data for MB’s cake options**

|   | **Option 1 Small cupcakes** | **Option 2 Large birthday cakes** |
| --- | :---: | :---: |
| Monthly sales of cakes | 4000 | 100 |
| Variable cost per cake | \$0.50 | \$10 |
| Additional fixed cost per month | \$3000 | \$3000 |
| Price per cake | \$2 per cupcake | \$60 per birthday cake |
| Gross profit margin | 75% | 83.33% |
| Sales growth | Low | High |

{align=center} 

{align=center} **Appendix 3 **

{align=center} **Packaging supplier advertisement**

{align=center} We only supply packaging made from sustainable sources. This will keep your products fresh and protect the environment. We can deliver your packaging when you need it.

Consider the following **two **ways MB could achieve lean production.

- Kaizen.
- Just-in-time inventory control.

Which is the best way for Yasin to choose? Justify your answer.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/09/jun-2022-paper-2-case-study---new.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solution_md:
Kaizen could involve Yasin and his two bakery employees constantly looking for ways to improve how they make bread **[Ap]**. For example, they might reorganise the small bakery** [Ap] **layout to reduce wasted movement between tasks, increasing productivity. This would allow them to make more bread each day, potentially increasing revenue **[An]**. However, Kaizen requires everyone to be motivated to suggest improvements. Yasin's minimum wage employees **[Ap]**, may not want to help if it means their hours get reduced due to increased efficiency **[An]**

Just-in-time inventory control would involve Yasin only ordering ingredients like flour **[Ap] **when needed. This could reduce storage costs in MB's small shop and bakery area and ensure ingredients are always fresh. As MainCity Bakery makes bread daily to sell in their shop, JIT could work well with this production cycle **[An]**. However, delays in ingredient deliveries could disrupt bread production and lead to lost sales **[An]**, which is risky for such a new business focused on increasing revenue **[Ap]**

Just-in-time inventory control is the best option **[E]**. As a small bakery making products daily, reducing storage while ensuring freshness is crucial **[E]**. While Kaizen could bring benefits, it may be harder to implement with just three employees who might resist changes **[E]**. JIT aligns with MainCity Bakery's production cycle and its need to keep costs low as a new business that received government help **[Ap]** to start up. Yasin should focus on building relationships with suppliers to make JIT work effectively, which could also help improve MB's ethical image **[Ap]** by sourcing local ingredients **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Kaizen**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Staff suggest tiny changes **→** smoother flow in the bakery **→** less wasted time and ingredients
>     - Shorter gaps between mixing → baking → cooling **→** higher output per hour
>     - Fewer half-finished trays lying around **→** tidier workspace and lower waste
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Only two workers; they might lack ideas or fear job cuts **→** little motivation to help
>     - Rearranging ovens and benches costs time or cash—hard for a start-up
>     - Yasin may need outside expertise to redesign the layout **→** extra short-term expense
>     - After the easy wins, further gains get smaller
> - **Just-in-time stock control**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Flour, yeast, sugar arrive just before use **→** less money tied up in stock and lower storage costs
>     - Fresher ingredients **→** tastier bread and cakes **→** happier customers
>     - No excess stock **→** nothing goes stale or out-of-date
>     - Space saved on shelves can be used for more production or a display counter
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Sudden jump in demand **→** not enough ingredients to meet orders
>     - Late supplier deliveries **→** production stops until stock arrives
>     - Relies on strong, fast communication with suppliers; Yasin must place frequent orders
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - Kaizen can boost efficiency and output but needs time, possible expert help, and willing staff
>   - JIT frees scarce cash and keeps ingredients fresh, yet it makes the bakery vulnerable to supplier delays
>   - Yasin should judge how reliable his ingredient suppliers are and how much cash he can spare before deciding to adopt one method, the other, or a mix of both

parts.problem_md:
Explain **two **factors DSY should consider when deciding on a suitable method of production for the new product.

> **[case-study]**
> DSY is a private limited company. It produces washing machines and cleaning equipment. The Managing Director wants DSY to expand into a different market. He plans to spend \$2bn on developing electric cars. There is a lot of competition in the electric car market. This market is growing rapidly. A leading pressure group has identified the environmental problems of non-electric cars. The Managing Director knows that important decisions about the method of production and the new car’s brand image still have to be made.
parts.solution_md:
DSY should consider the level of demand **[K]** when choosing a production method for electric cars. The market is growing rapidly **[Ap]**, suggesting high demand. This could make flow production suitable, as it allows efficient, large-scale production of standardised cars. This could help DSY keep costs down in the competitive electric car market** [An]**

Another factor is the nature of the product **[K]**. Electric cars are complex and may need specialised components **[Ap]**. Batch production might work well, letting DSY make groups of cars with similar features. This method offers some flexibility to customise different batches while being more efficient than job production** [An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Give two full points, one for each part of the question
> - For each point:
> 
>   - State a valid point relevant to the question → 1 K mark
>   - Apply it clearly to the business in the case study → 1 Ap mark
>   - Explain the impact using a cause–effect chain → 1 An mark
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Access to/amount of capital available/cost of machinery [k] as may not be able to afford to set up flow production [an] when already planning to spend \$2bn [app]
>   - Level of demand/size of market/volume needed [k] as there is a lot of competition [app] may not be able to sell/need to produce a large number [an]
>   - Nature/type of product [k] as cars [app] are more likely to be mass produced to be more cost-efficient/if luxury then job production might be suitable [an]
>   - Access to/amount of suitable space (inside the factory) [k]
>   - Access to (suitable/skilled) employees [k]
>   - Possible environmental damage/impact/pollution [k] which leads to protests by pressure groups [app] which could damage its reputation/ potential sales [an]
>   - How efficient is the method of production/amount of waste [k]
>   - Other appropriate responses should also be credited
> - The following words are likely to be appropriate for this question:
> 
>   - (electric) cars
>   - Washing machines/ cleaning equipment
>   - Lot of competition
>   - \$2bn
>   - Market is growing rapidly
>   - Pressure groups

**The BB Health Spa (BB)**

Bethany owns The BB Health Spa in Main City in country X. Economic growth has been high for the last few years. The government of country X wants this growth to continue so it has reduced income tax. However, it is also worried about inflation becoming a problem so it has increased interest rates.

The BB Health Spa is very busy and Bethany is considering taking on a partner to help manage the business and give her more free time. However, she has been a sole trader for 10 years and wants the business to stay small.

The customers of The BB Health Spa are people of all ages who are interested in their health. Bethany employs two qualified workers to provide the treatments for customers. Bethany herself also provides customers with treatments. In addition, she does all the administration such as ordering inventory, accounts and paying invoices when the spa is closed.

The BB Health Spa still uses the original treatment equipment which was purchased when the business started. Some spas nearby have the latest equipment but these spas charge much higher prices than The BB Health Spa. Bethany records all the financial transactions by filling in accounts books by hand. This takes her a long time. Customers book appointments using the telephone and Bethany later telephones them to remind them when an appointment is due.

parts.problem_md:
Explain **two **possible problems for TBX of holding a high level of inventory.

> **[case-study]**
> TBX manufactures high-quality steel, which is used to build railways. The method of production used allows TBX to benefit from economies of scale. The business holds a high level of inventory, including iron ore. The Managing Director knows business activity could have an impact on the environment and is considering ways the business can contribute to sustainable development.
parts.solution_md:
Storing large amounts of iron ore requires expensive warehouse space **[K]**. This increases TBX's overhead costs and ties up working capital that could be used for other purposes, like investing in new steel-making equipment **[Ap]**. As a manufacturer benefiting from economies of scale, TBX likely already has significant fixed costs, so additional storage expenses could hurt profitability **[An]**

If TBX keeps too much inventory for too long, some iron ore may degrade in quality or become unusable **[K]**. This is particularly risky for raw materials in heavy industry. TBX could end up with worthless stock, leading to write-offs and wasted resources. This contradicts the goal of sustainable development **[Ap] **that the Managing Director is considering **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Give two full points, one for each part of the question
> - For each point:
> 
>   - State a valid point relevant to the question → 1 K mark
>   - Apply it clearly to the business in the case study → 1 Ap mark
>   - Explain the impact using a cause–effect chain → 1 An mark
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Rent/storage space/large space needed [k] for the steel [app] which can increase fixed costs/expenses [an]
>   - Ties up working capital [k] such as iron ore [app] which could lead to liquidity/cash flow problems/difficult to pay suppliers [an]
>   - Insurance costs [k] which increase cash outflows [an] so less funds to contribute to sustainable development [app]
>   - Opportunity cost/funds could be used for other purposes [k]
>   - Risk of damage/theft/wastage/product could rust [k] leading to higher costs [an]
>   - Other appropriate responses should be credited
> - The following words are likely to be appropriate for this question:
> 
>   - Steel
>   - Railways
>   - Iron (ore)
>   - High-quality
>   - Sustainable  development/impact on environment

parts.problem_md: Do you think improving labour skills is the best way for a manufacturing business to increase efficiency? Justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Improving labour skills by training workers can help them work faster and make fewer mistakes **[K]**, leading to higher output and less waste. However, training takes time and increases costs in the short-term, which could lower efficiency initially **[An]**

Other methods like automation or lean production might be better. Automation allows operation with fewer employees **[K]**, potentially increasing efficiency more than training. Lean production, such as Just-in-Time, can lower costs per unit, improving overall efficiency **[An]**

While improving labour skills is valuable, it's not always the best way to increase efficiency in manufacturing **[E]**. If the main issue is worker productivity, improving skills might be best. However, if the problem is high costs or excess inventory, lean production could be more effective **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - You are writing a mini-argument with a decision
> 
>   - Give one relevant reason to support your view → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this reason helps the business (cause-effect chain) →  1 An mark
>   - Give a different possible reason or viewpoint → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this could also help the business → 1 An mark
>   - Make a decision — which argument is stronger or more important overall? → up to 2 E marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Job production:
>   
>     - Meet exact customer requirements [k] which increases customer loyalty/sales [an]
>     - Unique/high-quality products [k] can charge higher price [an]
>     - Products made to order/can take a long time to make [k] so low output [an]
>     - No economies of scale [k] leading to higher average cost [an]
>     - Skilled labour is needed [k] increases labour/training costs [an]
>     - Requires a lot of employees/labour intensive [k]
>   - Batch production [k]:
>   
>     - Some economies of scale [an]
>     - Able to produce more [an] so unit costs lower [an]
>     - Can produce range/variety of products [an]
>     - Demotivated employees [an] increasing labour turnover [an]
>     - Machines must be reset between batches [an]
>     - Added cost of moving/storing semi-finished goods [an]
>     - Warehouse space is needed [an]/increases storage costs [an]

> 
>   - increased productivity

>   - lower cost
>   - more output

parts.problem_md: Do you think job production is the best method of production for a small business to use? Justify your answer.

Job production allows small businesses to make unique, high-quality products that exactly meet customer needs **[K]**. This can help build customer loyalty and allow them to charge higher prices **[An]**.

However, job production requires skilled workers, which may be expensive to employ, increasing labour costs **[K]**. It also takes longer to make products, leading to lower output. This means the business can't benefit from economies of scale, so their average costs stay high **[An]**

For a small business focused on customised, premium products for a niche market, job production could be ideal. But for a small business aiming to compete on price or needing to produce large quantities quickly, batch or flow production might work better **[E]**. The best method depends on the business's goals, target market, and available resources **[E]**

parts.problem_md:
Explain **two **methods TYA could use to increase efficiency.

> **[case-study]**
> TYA is a limited company which manufactures 300 000 cars a year. It has 600 employees. TYA has high fixed costs. The Managing Director wants to improve efficiency in the factory. He said: ‘Globalisation is changing how businesses operate. Many manufacturing businesses are considering whether to relocate their operations to other countries.’
parts.solution_md:
TYA could introduce automation in its factory** [K]**. This would allow the company to produce cars faster and potentially reduce labour costs **[An] **among its 600 employees** [Ap]**. Automation could involve using robots or computer-controlled machinery on the production line. This may help TYA lower its high fixed costs over time** [An]**

Another method is implementing just-in-time inventory control **[K]**. This lean production technique would reduce the amount of parts and materials stored in TYA's factory **[An]**. With less inventory, TYA could use its factory space more efficiently to manufacture its 300,000 cars per year **[Ap]**, which may reduce its high fixed costs **[An]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Give two full points, one for each part of the question
> - For each point:
> 
>   - State a valid point relevant to the question → 1 K mark
>   - Apply it clearly to the business in the case study → 1 Ap mark
>   - Explain the impact using a cause–effect chain → 1 An mark
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Increase in capital intensity / automation / introduce new technology [k] increasing output / faster production [an] of cars [app]

parts.problem_md: Do you think flow production is the best method of production for a manufacturing business to use? Justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Flow production allows for high output, helping businesses meet large demand efficiently **[K]**. Flow production also benefits from economies of scale and it's often more capital intensive, leading to lower unit costs. This can give the business a competitive advantage as these lower costs can be passed on to consumers as lower prices **[An]**

However, flow production  requires a large capital investment upfront, which not all businesses can afford. If one machine breaks down, the whole production line stops **[K]**, potentially causing significant drops in output. This may mean that business cannot meet deadlines for orders, and its customers may buy from a rival instead **[An]**

For manufacturing businesses producing standardised products with high, consistent demand, flow production is likely the best method. It allows them to maximise efficiency and minimise costs **[E]**. However, for businesses with varied product lines or fluctuating demand, batch or job production may be more suitable. The choice ultimately depends on the nature of the product, market demand, and available capital **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - You are writing a mini-argument with a decision
> 
>   - Give one relevant reason to support your view → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this reason helps the business (cause-effect chain) →  1 An mark
>   - Give a different possible reason or viewpoint → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this could also help the business → 1 An mark
>   - Make a decision — which argument is stronger or more important overall? → up to 2 E marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - High output [k] so able to meet demand (on time) [an]
>   - Benefit from economies of scale [k] leading to lower unit costs [an]
>   - More capital intensive [k] leading to lower labour costs [an]
>   - Lower (employee) motivation [k] leading to lower productivity [an]
>   - Can produce 24 hours a day [k]
>   - If one machine breaks down whole production line stops [k] lose output/fewer sales [an]
>   - Requires a large capital investment [k]
>   - Batch production [k]
>   - More flexible / produce a variety of products [an]
>   - Job production [k]
>   - Unique products so able to charge a higher price [an]
>   - Other appropriate responses should also be credited
> - Justification might include:
> 
>   - Materials can be purchased in large amounts / benefit from economies of scale [k] leading to lower unit costs [an]. However, it requires a large capital investment [k] which the business might not be able to afford. [an] It might only be worthwhile if there is a large market for a standardised product [eval] which can cover the high initial costs [eval]

parts.problem_md: Do you think the ways technology has changed production methods benefit all employees? Justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
On the positive side, technology can make jobs safer and more enjoyable **[K] **by automating dangerous tasks, which means employees are less likely to be injured at work.  It also creates opportunities for workers to learn new skills, which may open up opportunities for promotion, leading to higher pay **[An]**

Overall, whether an employee benefits depends on their ability to adapt. Workers who gain new technical skills are more likely to benefit, while those unable to adjust often struggle **[E]**. Given these mixed impacts, businesses should focus on helping all employees transition as technology changes production. This could include retraining programmes and gradually introducing new technologies. With the right approach, the benefits of new production methods can be more widely shared **[E]**

parts.problem_md:
Outline** one** advantage and **one** disadvantage to NSN of using just-in-time inventory control.

> **[case-study]**
> NSN is a multinational company. It makes cars. Over the years, technology has changed production methods. NSN uses just-in-time inventory control in all its factories. NSN plans to open a new factory in country Z, creating 7 000 jobs. Country Z’s Government has offered an \$80m grant to NSN. A spokesperson for NSN said: ‘Governments should support business activity. There were also other factors that influenced our decision to build the new factory there, including the possible effects of economic growth.’
parts.solution_md:
Less warehouse space **[K] **is needed to store the parts for manufacturing cars **[Ap]**

NSN will be more dependent on suppliers **[K]** to deliver stock when needed as technology has changed how production is carried out **[Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Knowledge 2; Application 2
> 
>   - Give two valid ways to classify the business to achieve both knowledge [K] marks
>   - For each way, refer to the business case study to achieve both application [Ap] marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Advantages:
>   
>     - Less warehouse space [k] needed to store parts for cars [app]
>     - Less inventory held [k] in its factories [ap]
>     - Lower storage costs [k] for the multinational company [Ap]
>     - Improve working capital [k]
>     - Improve cash flow [k]
>     - Lower risk of obsolete/damaged stock [k]
>   - Disadvantages:
>   
>     - Very reliant on suppliers to deliver stock when needed / if parts not available / late it will have a major impact on production [k] as technology has changed how production is carried out [app]
>     - May not be able to meet sudden/unexpected order [k]
>     - Little room for mistakes (as minimal stock available for rework) [k]
>     - Less (purchasing) economies of scale [k]

>   - Technology changed production
